# The mathematical language of quantum science

*General graduate reference · original educational exposition · no project-specific data used as universal physics.*


![A fully coherent two-level state represented by its Bloch-sphere angles (original educational diagram)](../../site/assets/book-quantum-bloch.svg)

*Original scientifically labelled illustration; pedagogical geometry rather than acquired atomic data.*

## Learning goals

Develop the physical and mathematical background to derive a model, choose observables, test its limiting cases and recognise invalid numerical results. Prerequisites: complex numbers, linear algebra, calculus and SI units. See the [scholarly bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

## 1. What a quantum state actually represents

In a complex Hilbert space the state |ψ⟩ is a unit vector up to a physically irrelevant common phase. For |ψ⟩=a|g⟩+b|e⟩, |a|²+|b|²=1 and measurement in the {|g⟩,|e⟩} basis produces probabilities |a|² and |b|². Complex amplitudes are not the same as the measured voltage from a detector. Relative phase changes interference in a rotated basis, while multiplying both amplitudes by e^{iφ} does not change an expectation value. One should distinguish a pure state, the state vector used to represent it, and a classical ensemble in which the same apparatus prepares different states on different runs.

## 2. Dirac notation and the Born rule

A ket |ψ⟩ is a column vector and its bra ⟨ψ| is the conjugate transpose. An inner product ⟨a|b⟩ describes overlap; it is generally complex. For a normalized projector P=|a⟩⟨a|, the probability of its outcome is ⟨ψ|P|ψ⟩=|⟨a|ψ⟩|². The identity resolution ∑_i |i⟩⟨i|=I holds for a *complete orthonormal* basis. It does not hold for an arbitrary set of nonorthogonal candidates. Real optical experiments acquire ensemble fluorescence or probe transmission, not single-state Born-rule outcomes directly. A forward optical model is needed between microscopic state and macroscopic data.

## 3. Basis rotations, phase and polarisation

A unitary U satisfies U†U=I; it transforms state coordinates as |ψ⟩new=U†|ψ⟩ and observables as Anew=U†AU. Expectations are unchanged, which is a valuable software regression test. For light or RF fields the Cartesian (x,y) basis and the spherical (π,σ±) basis are different coordinate descriptions of the same vector, with helicity sign determined by propagation and time convention. A phase error of π/2 can interchange a linear and circular basis inference. Write down the transformation explicitly before passing complex field components between optical Bloch, atomic-dipole and antenna codes.

## 4. Linear algebra for inverse science

The singular value decomposition A=UΣV† is defined for a rectangular matrix and reveals which parameter combinations are invisible or ill-conditioned. Rank identifies whether a noiseless solution can be unique; a small σmin controls amplification of some perturbations. A numerical condition number only has meaning after declaring units, column scaling and weighting. A transfer matrix mapping incident polarisation into an optical detector does not automatically become a quantum measurement operator. Distinguish the physical process from the numerical instrument-response linearization.

## 5. Calculus and coherent evolution

For a time-independent Hermitian Hamiltonian H the propagator is exp(−iHt/ℏ); its Taylor series involves matrix powers, not element-by-element exponentials. A diagonal Hamiltonian gives each energy eigencomponent a phase exp(−iEjt/ℏ), and interference depends on differences Ej−Ek. For a time-dependent H(t), a single exponential of its integral is invalid unless the Hamiltonians commute at different times. A numerical integrator should preserve norm in a genuinely closed system. Unit-normalised output can still be physically wrong if a time step misses rapid micromotion or if an angular frequency was supplied as cycles/s.

## 6. Statistics and uncertainty with real laboratory data

An average reduces independent, zero-mean noise, but it does not remove systematic calibration error. The sample standard deviation describes scatter; the standard error describes uncertainty of the estimated mean, and a naive 1/√N law fails for serially correlated laser scans. Covariance matters when the same frequency lock, temperature monitor or reference power affects several data channels. Record detector bandwidth and readout gains before comparing datasets. A photodetector output, atomic state variance and RF-field inference uncertainty are three different quantities.

## 7. Worked derivation and numerical checks

Let |ψ⟩=(|0⟩+i|1⟩)/√2. Measuring Z gives p(0)=p(1)=1/2. The Y-basis eigenstate |+y⟩=(|0⟩+i|1⟩)/√2 has overlap 1 and the opposite eigenstate has overlap zero, so ⟨σy⟩=1. Multiply |ψ⟩ by i and repeat: all probabilities stay unchanged. Now replace i with −i; Z-basis probabilities are still equal, but ⟨σy⟩=−1. Thus population measurements in a single basis cannot determine relative phase. Verify all calculations with explicit 2×2 Pauli matrices and complex conjugation in code.

## 8. Experiment-to-model checklist

Before a calculation: (1) state the physical observable and acquisition chain; (2) define your basis, signs and units; (3) write at least one analytically solvable limit; (4) test a change of coordinates; (5) check numerical conservation laws; (6) vary step size or discretisation; (7) record dependencies and raw inputs; (8) distinguish a simulation, measurement and algebraic illustration. These checks apply to virtually every Rydberg apparatus, from Stark spectroscopy to tweezer-array blockade.

## End-of-chapter questions and fully explained answers

### Problem 1. Why can no single-basis population measurement recover relative phase?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It squares amplitudes independently. Phase appears in interference terms once a noncommuting measurement basis mixes them.

</details>

### Problem 2. Which numerical method identifies weakly observable parameters in a six-by-four instrument matrix?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Singular-value decomposition, together with a declared noise metric and column scaling.

</details>

### Problem 3. What changes under a global phase e^{iφ}?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

State-vector representation changes but all density matrices and measurement probabilities remain unchanged.

</details>

### Problem 4. Why can a good-looking fit have an invalid uncertainty?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Errors may be correlated, the model may be biased, and fit residuals may violate the assumed likelihood.

</details>

### Problem 5. What is an essential unit check on a Hamiltonian?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

All matrix entries must represent the same physical quantity, typically joules or ℏ times angular frequency.

</details>

### Problem 6. Why do inverse-problem condition numbers depend on scaling?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Rescaling parameters or observations changes singular values and their ratio; dimensioned variables must be normalized meaningfully.

</details>

### Problem 7. What must hold for a closed-system numerical propagator?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It should be approximately unitary and preserve the norm of every input state, with errors controlled by a stated tolerance.

</details>

### Problem 8. How can one test a basis transform implementation?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Compute an observable in both frames and show numerical invariance of its expectation under consistent state and operator transformations.

</details>

## Advanced practical assignment

Implement a minimal self-contained version of the chapter's central equation. Supply its units, analytic limiting cases, a second independent check, and a reproducible test that fails when a sign or unit is changed. Distinguish generated illustrations from laboratory data. Explain how the model would be extended to a specific atomic species *only after* those foundations are correct.

## References

Use [F1] Foot, [Q1] Scully and Zubairy, [F2] Steck's Quantum and Atom Optics and the numerical analysis sources in [the bibliography](../REFERENCES.md). Consult original primary publications before reusing a parameter as experimental evidence.


## Extended derivation: interference from complex amplitudes

A complex number is not an optional decoration on a classical probability. Its phase determines how alternative quantum pathways combine. Suppose a system admits two alternative coherent paths from its initial state to a final measurement state, contributing amplitudes a₁ and a₂. The probability is |a₁+a₂|²=|a₁|²+|a₂|²+2Re(a₁a₂*). The final interference term is absent from the classical sum of two exclusive probabilities. Therefore adding probabilities prematurely destroys experimentally observable relative-phase effects. When laser-induced coherence and microwave-induced coupling participate in a Rydberg spectroscopic feature, this distinction is central: the optical probe signal can respond to phase-sensitive atomic coherences, even though the final photodetector output is real.

Take a₁=1/2 and a₂=e^{iφ}/2. Then the interference probability is (1+cosφ)/2, varying from 0 to 1 as relative phase changes. Multiplying both amplitudes by the same e^{iθ} leaves this probability unchanged. An optical intensity measurement is often insensitive to the overall optical phase, whereas a heterodyne measurement with a known reference can convert a relative phase into a detected intensity oscillation. Identifying what is measurable requires specifying the reference, not simply writing a complex state.

## Extended derivation: uncertainty and compatible measurements

For Hermitian A and B, define centred operators ΔA=A−⟨A⟩ and ΔB=B−⟨B⟩. Cauchy–Schwarz applied to ΔA|ψ⟩ and ΔB|ψ⟩ yields ΔA²ΔB²≥|⟨ΔA ΔB⟩|². The imaginary part of this covariance is ⟨[A,B]⟩/(2i), yielding the Robertson lower bound ΔAΔB≥|⟨[A,B]⟩|/2. This lower bound can be zero even for noncommuting operators when the particular state makes the expected commutator zero; a zero bound does not imply all observables can be known sharply in that state.

For spin-1/2, [σx,σy]=2iσz. In an eigenstate of σz with eigenvalue +1, the variances of σx and σy both equal one, saturating the spin-form bound ΔσxΔσy≥1. But an experimental detector's output voltage may have far larger variance due to electronic and environmental noise, and calibration uncertainty is a separate systematic component. Do not label all observed noise “quantum uncertainty.” In practice, shot noise, projection noise, laser phase noise and classical technical noise require different likelihood models.

## Extended derivation: change of basis without changing physics

Let the computational basis be |g⟩=(1,0)^T and |e⟩=(0,1)^T. Define |+⟩=(|g⟩+|e⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|g⟩−|e⟩)/√2. The unitary whose columns are these new basis states is U=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]]. To represent the same physical state in the new coordinates, use |ψ⟩new=U†|ψ⟩. The operator must transform consistently as Anew=U†AU. The expectation ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ is then invariant because U U†=I. Transforming the state but not the operator produces spurious dependence on software basis ordering.

A numerical regression test should choose a random normalised state, a Hermitian observable and a known unitary, then check expectation invariance within tolerance. Repeat with a complex rotation, not only a real matrix, so a missing conjugation is caught. The same reasoning becomes crucial for atomic spherical bases: a field written in laboratory x/y components does not directly determine q=±1 coupling strengths until it is transformed relative to the magnetic quantisation axis.

## Extended derivation: density operators as probabilities over preparations

A source that produces state |ψₖ⟩ with classical probability pₖ is represented by ρ=Σₖpₖ|ψₖ⟩⟨ψₖ|. For any observable A, the ensemble mean is Tr(ρA). A different ensemble decomposition can produce the same ρ and is therefore indistinguishable using only measurements on the system. This is a crucial identifiability limit: what a model calls its constituent “preparations” need not be uniquely inferred from the measured optical response.

For a two-level system, ρ=(I+r·σ)/2 with real Bloch vector r and |r|≤1. A pure state has |r|=1 and Tr(ρ²)=1; the maximally mixed state has r=0 and purity 1/2. A fitted Bloch vector with norm above one implies a nonphysical state unless the reported quantities are not actually normalised Bloch coordinates. This mathematical physicality test can be applied before any specific atomic species is introduced.

## Extended derivation: forward and inverse problems

Suppose a system maps unknown parameter θ to measured data y through y=f(θ)+ε. A forward model predicts y for a known θ. An inverse model estimates θ given y. In general f may not be one-to-one. If two parameter sets produce the same observable, no amount of noiseless repetition can distinguish them without an additional measurement basis or prior restriction. In linear form y=Aθ, full column rank is necessary for unique noiseless inversion. Even when rank is complete, singular values close to zero make inversion unstable.

This has two distinct implications for Rydberg systems. First, an optical spectrum may depend on combinations of RF amplitude, detuning, linewidth and atomic density; fitting one spectrum can therefore produce correlated parameters. Second, spatially and polarisation-resolved measurements may require multiple independent configurations before a vector field can be recovered. A clever optimiser cannot create information absent from the forward map. A researcher should inspect parameter identifiability through a Jacobian ∂f/∂θ or a physically motivated Fisher matrix and then design new measurements to resolve the weak directions.

## Unit discipline and dimensional reasoning

Every numerical routine should decide whether the state evolution Hamiltonian is expressed in joules, angular frequency rad/s or cycle frequency Hz. If H is in joules, iℏd|ψ⟩/dt=H|ψ⟩. If the reduced Hamiltonian H/ℏ is in rad/s, its eigenvalues are angular rates. A detuning reported as 10 MHz often means Δω=2π×10⁷ rad/s, but a software package may instead define internal detunings in multiples of 2π MHz or scaled units. The correct procedure is to inspect official documentation, trace the conversion and test a known Rabi period.

Dimensional consistency is an inexpensive but powerful diagnostic. The matrix element dE has dimensions (C·m)(V/m)=J. Dividing by ℏ gives s⁻¹ (angular frequency), while dividing by h gives Hz. A reported coherence time is not a frequency; its inverse has frequency dimensions, with numerical π/2 factors depending on how linewidth is defined (amplitude decay, population decay, FWHM). Using generic “gamma=1” values without units prevents a reproducible line-shape prediction.

## Further extended exercises

<details><summary>Q9. Two coherent paths have amplitudes 0.3 and 0.4 e^{iφ}. Find the probability for φ=0 and φ=π.</summary>

For φ=0, P=|0.7|²=0.49. For φ=π, P=|−0.1|²=0.01. Adding separate probabilities would give 0.09+0.16=0.25 and miss interference. These amplitudes may be components of an outcome within a larger normalised state; their total is not automatically a complete measurement probability distribution.

</details>

<details><summary>Q10. Compute the purity of a diagonal qubit state with probabilities 0.8 and 0.2.</summary>

Tr(ρ²)=0.8²+0.2²=0.68. Because the purity is below one, it is mixed. A different physical classical preparation may produce the same density operator.

</details>

<details><summary>Q11. Transform σz into the |+⟩,|−⟩ basis.</summary>

Using the Hadamard U above, U†σzU=σx. The state coordinates must also transform. Computing the same expectation in both bases gives equal values.

</details>

<details><summary>Q12. Explain why a measured 10 MHz line splitting is not automatically a Rabi angular rate of 10 million rad/s.</summary>

The frequency splitting is in cycles/s. If the simple resonant model maps that splitting directly to Ω/(2π), Ω would be 2π×10⁷ rad/s. In an actual multilevel, Doppler-broadened atomic spectrum, the mapping must be verified and may not be exact.

</details>

<details><summary>Q13. A computed Bloch vector is (0.7,0.8,0.2). Is it physical?</summary>

Its squared norm is 0.49+0.64+0.04=1.17, exceeding one. A qubit density matrix built as (I+r·σ)/2 would have a negative eigenvalue. Inspect normalisation or inversion errors rather than clipping silently.

</details>

<details><summary>Q14. Give a concrete criterion for when an inverse model cannot uniquely identify its parameters.</summary>

If f(θ₁)=f(θ₂) for distinct admissible θ₁,θ₂, then y=f(θ) does not uniquely identify the input. For a linear model this is equivalent to a nontrivial nullspace of A: A v=0 with v≠0.

</details>

<details><summary>Q15. Why does increasing the sample count not necessarily fix a nonidentifiable experiment?</summary>

Repeating an identical measurement can reduce statistical variance but cannot resolve a missing independent response direction. Change the measurement basis, geometry, time dependence or reference observable.

</details>

<details><summary>Q16. Derive the photon energy for 780 nm and report eV.</summary>

E=hc/λ=(6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s)(299792458 m/s)/(780×10⁻⁹ m)≈2.546×10⁻¹⁹ J. Divide by 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J/eV to obtain ≈1.589 eV.

</details>

<details><summary>Q17. Why does a unitary basis change preserve density-matrix purity?</summary>

ρ'=U†ρU and Tr((ρ')²)=Tr(U†ρUU†ρU)=Tr(U†ρ²U)=Tr(ρ²) by unitarity and cyclic trace. A numerical purity discrepancy indicates an implementation or rounding problem.

</details>

<details><summary>Q18. What mathematical feature reveals poor parameter sensitivity near a best fit?</summary>

Small singular values of the Jacobian or a near-singular Fisher information matrix indicate directions along which the observable changes little. The precise interpretation depends on the likelihood, scaling and nuisance parameters.

</details>

<details><summary>Q19. Can a state have no intrinsic spin-uncertainty in σz and also no uncertainty in σx?</summary>

Not as a pure simultaneous eigenstate of both noncommuting Pauli operators. A σz eigenstate has a definite z outcome but an equal distribution of x outcomes; Δσx=1.

</details>

<details><summary>Q20. What independent software regression would catch a missing complex conjugation?</summary>

Compare ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ in two randomly chosen complex unitary bases using U† on both state and operator. A transpose in place of conjugate transpose generally breaks expectation invariance.

</details>

## Expanded references

- Foot, *Atomic Physics*, Oxford University Press, for state and measurement foundations.
- Scully and Zubairy, *Quantum Optics*, Cambridge University Press, for density operators and coherent optical interference.
- Steck, *Quantum and Atom Optics*, https://steck.us/teaching/ for detailed graduate quantum methodology.
- Golub and Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, for rank, singular values and numerical stability.

title: Operators, observables and quantum measurement

# Operators, observables and quantum measurement

**General atomic and quantum physics textbook.** The treatment is not a project-specific apparatus description. Physics constants and state labels must be verified for each chosen species.

## Learning objectives

Derive the central equations, quantify assumptions, compute a simple limiting case, plan an independent experiment and diagnose numerical or laboratory errors.

## 1. Spectral theorem and eigenprojectors

Every finite-dimensional Hermitian observable A admits a spectral decomposition A=∑a_kP_k. Projectors P_k are positive, mutually orthogonal and sum to identity. The probability of outcome k is Tr(ρP_k), and expectation is Tr(ρA). Degeneracy changes the rank of P_k, not the Born rule. Measuring a single basis is generally informationally incomplete: many different coherences yield the same populations. Distinguish a microscopic quantum observable from the measured macroscopic signal, which includes a detector and a forward model.

## 2. Noncommuting observables and uncertainty

The commutator [A,B]=AB−BA determines the Robertson bound ΔAΔB≥|⟨[A,B]⟩|/2. The full Schrödinger uncertainty relation includes covariance and is stronger in many states. The bound is state dependent and should not be confused with classical sampling uncertainty or optical detector noise. One may have very precise technical frequency estimation without preparing an energy eigenstate, because the measurement can integrate coherent signals from many atoms.

## 3. Generalised measurements and loss

Positive operator-valued measures E_k≥0, ∑E_k=I describe detectors with outcomes that need not correspond to orthogonal projections. A finite-efficiency photon detector can be modelled through a calibrated response and losses; including dark counts or saturation may require an extended classical likelihood. An uncalibrated optical current is not an atom state probability. Always state where the atomic model ends and the detector model begins.

## 4. Uncertainty propagation and Fisher information

For an observation y=f(θ)+ε, local parameter sensitivity is J=∂f/∂θ. If ε is Gaussian with covariance C, the local Fisher matrix is F=JᵀC⁻¹J when C is parameter independent. F being invertible is not sufficient for a useful estimator if one eigenvalue is tiny. Spectral noise density has units per square-root bandwidth for amplitude noise and must be integrated through the actual filter; correlations invalidate naive sample-count scaling.

## 5. A worked two-level statistics example

For ρ=diag(0.7,0.3), a σz measurement has mean 0.4, second moment 1 and variance 0.84. If 1000 independently re-prepared atoms are measured, standard deviation of their average is √(0.84/1000)=0.02898. If 1000 recorded detector samples share laser drift, this number is not valid. An honest estimate measures autocorrelation or effective sample size and includes systematic calibration separately.

## 6. Measurement design checklist

Identify whether the desired output is a quantum probability, classical current, phase, spectral frequency or inferred field. Choose a primary physical control, a calibrated detector reference and an independent second measurement basis if phase or vector information is required. Preserve original shots and timestamps, not only an averaged graph. Do not interpret a model's minimum variance as measured sensitivity before testing with laboratory noise.

## End-of-chapter review questions and worked answers

### Question 1. What makes E_k a valid POVM effect?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

It is positive semidefinite, and all effects sum to identity.

</details>

### Question 2. Why is a single projection basis incomplete?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Off-diagonal phases may not affect its populations but change predictions in another basis.

</details>

### Question 3. Does Robertson uncertainty specify the photodiode noise floor?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

No, it constrains state-observable variances, not electronic or laser noise.

</details>

### Question 4. How does correlation change averaging?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Shared noise reduces effective independent sample number, weakening the 1/√N scaling.

</details>

### Question 5. What determines whether F is useful?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Its eigenvalues in the calibrated noise and parameter-unit metric, not invertibility alone.

</details>

### Question 6. Why is measurement calibration a model component?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Physical states map to voltages or counts through finite efficiency, gain, bandwidth and backgrounds.

</details>

## Graduate practical problem

Develop a reproducible calculation for the principal equation in this chapter, record coordinate frame and units, compare against a separate source or an analytically solvable limit, and describe a controlled measurement that could falsify the model. Explicitly distinguish a derived teaching example from new experimental evidence.

## Scholarly sources

See [the textbook bibliography](../REFERENCES.md), Gallagher (*Rydberg Atoms*), Foot (*Atomic Physics*), Scully and Zubairy (*Quantum Optics*), and official atomic spectroscopy data when applying formulas to an actual species.

title: Hamiltonians, rotating frames and coherent control

# Hamiltonians, rotating frames and coherent control

**General atomic and quantum physics textbook.** The treatment is not a project-specific apparatus description. Physics constants and state labels must be verified for each chosen species.

## Learning objectives

Derive the central equations, quantify assumptions, compute a simple limiting case, plan an independent experiment and diagnose numerical or laboratory errors.

## 1. The interaction Hamiltonian

Begin with H=H0−d·E(t). The dipole moment d is an operator; its matrix elements connect allowed atomic states according to angular-momentum selection rules. In a two-state rotating-wave model, H/ℏ can be written as (−Δσz+Ωσx)/2 after specifying basis order, phase and detuning sign. The Rabi frequency Ω is an angular rate in rad/s when H is divided by ℏ. A rotating frame changes coordinates but cannot change physical probabilities.

## 2. Where the RWA comes from

Expanding E0cos(ωt+φ) into exponentials produces near-resonant and counter-rotating terms. Transforming to a frame rotating with the laser reveals one slowly varying component and another rotating near twice the carrier. Neglect of the fast term is justified only if drive and detuning are sufficiently small compared with carrier frequency. Ultrastrong coupling, rapid modulation and Floquet-assisted Rydberg spectroscopy may require retaining counter-rotating dynamics.

## 3. Exact Rabi oscillations

For an atom initially in the lower state, P_e(t)=(Ω²/(Ω²+Δ²))sin²(√(Ω²+Δ²)t/2). The probability's first maximum is at t=π/√(Ω²+Δ²), not necessarily π/Ω; its height is reduced when Δ≠0. If Ω/2π=2 MHz and Δ/2π=1 MHz, the maximum is 0.8. A textbook calculation is not a measured time-domain Rydberg coherence; spontaneous decay, Doppler effects and finite atom motion may change the result.

## 4. Three-level coherence and dressed states

EIT and coherent population trapping arise from interference between excitation pathways. In an idealised lambda system a dark state proportional to Ωc|g⟩−Ωp|r⟩ decouples from a shared excited state at two-photon resonance. A ladder EIT system has its own decay and state structure; do not assume all lambda-system formulas transfer unchanged. Adding an RF-coupled fourth state modifies the dressed eigenvalues and can generate Autler–Townes features under suitable linewidth conditions.

## 5. Numerical propagation and error checks

For time-independent H, U(t)=exp(−iHt/ℏ) is unitary. For H(t), time-ordering is required if H at different times does not commute. Explicit integration must converge with step size, preserve norm in the closed limit and recover Ω→0, Δ→0 and far-detuned limits. When adding dissipation, transition to a density-matrix/Lindblad solver instead of manually renormalising a decaying wavefunction without a physical model.

## 6. Design and diagnosis

Build a drive-frequency/state diagram and write the actual sign of each complex coupling. Check selection rules, numerical angular-frequency conversions, phase references and branch choice. A simulated avoided crossing is not an experimental field calibration; spectroscopy requires independent frequency and detector controls.

## End-of-chapter review questions and worked answers

### Question 1. What is the difference between Ω and Ω/2π?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Ω is angular frequency in rad/s, while Ω/2π is cycles/s; mixing them creates an erroneous 2π.

</details>

### Question 2. Why does RWA fail for sufficiently strong RF?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Counter-rotating terms no longer average away and may modify energies or sidebands.

</details>

### Question 3. How much transfer occurs for Δ=Ω/2?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Maximum transfer is Ω²/(Ω²+Ω²/4)=0.8.

</details>

### Question 4. Can a three-state dark vector predict a full thermal spectrum?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

No; dissipative dynamics, Doppler classes, density and optical propagation must be added.

</details>

### Question 5. Which identity tests a propagator?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

U†U=I to numerical tolerance in a closed system.

</details>

### Question 6. Why are relative phases meaningful?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Coupled pathways interfere and their relative phases determine coherent probabilities.

</details>

## Graduate practical problem

Develop a reproducible calculation for the principal equation in this chapter, record coordinate frame and units, compare against a separate source or an analytically solvable limit, and describe a controlled measurement that could falsify the model. Explicitly distinguish a derived teaching example from new experimental evidence.

## Scholarly sources

See [the textbook bibliography](../REFERENCES.md), Gallagher (*Rydberg Atoms*), Foot (*Atomic Physics*), Scully and Zubairy (*Quantum Optics*), and official atomic spectroscopy data when applying formulas to an actual species.

title: Density matrices and open quantum systems
markdown:
# Density matrices and open quantum systems

*General graduate reference · original educational exposition · no project-specific data used as universal physics.*

## Learning goals

Develop the physical and mathematical background to derive a model, choose observables, test its limiting cases and recognise invalid numerical results. Prerequisites: complex numbers, linear algebra, calculus and SI units. See the [scholarly bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

## 1. Ensembles and positivity

A density operator ρ=∑pk|ψk⟩⟨ψk| represents an ensemble. It obeys ρ=ρ†, Trρ=1 and ρ≥0. The spectral decomposition of a density matrix expresses it as nonnegative eigenvalue weights, but there can be many other ensemble decompositions of the same physical state. Pure states satisfy Trρ²=1; mixed states generally have lower purity. Populations are diagonal matrix elements in a specified basis and coherences are off-diagonal elements. A population-only rate model cannot generally describe phase-sensitive electromagnetically induced transparency.

## 2. Derivation of coherent density evolution

Differentiate ρ=|ψ⟩⟨ψ| and substitute iℏ∂t|ψ⟩=H|ψ⟩. The result is dρ/dt=−i[H,ρ]/ℏ, where [H,ρ]=Hρ−ρH. The commutator conserves trace and purity. An energy offset proportional to identity does not alter ρ, explaining why absolute energy reference drops out of isolated coherent dynamics. For an optical ladder, different laser couplings create coherences across the relevant states, and their interference can profoundly change probe absorption.

## 3. Lindblad dissipators without hand-waving

A Markovian completely positive master equation adds D[L]ρ=LρL†−(L†Lρ+ρL†L)/2. For spontaneous decay |e⟩→|g⟩ at population decay rate Γ, choose L=√Γ|g⟩⟨e|. Then excited population decays at Γ, while optical coherence typically acquires Γ/2 from that channel. Pure dephasing may suppress coherences without redistributing populations. Be careful about packages that express line widths as half-widths, full widths, angular frequency or cycles per second. A model can be numerically stable and still be physically wrong if dissipators are assigned to the wrong states.

## 4. Stationary solutions, uniqueness and trace constraints

Steady state solves Lρ=0 together with Trρ=1. The Liouvillian superoperator has a zero eigenvalue in a trace-preserving dynamics, but there can be multiple stationary states if the graph is disconnected or preserves a nontrivial invariant subspace. A solver must impose trace independently and should report the residual of the original equation. To check physicality, evaluate the minimum eigenvalue, Hermiticity error and trace error. Small negative eigenvalues may arise from numerical roundoff; larger violations signal an invalid model or numerical failure, not an invitation to clamp the solution silently.

## 5. From atomic coherence to optical transmission

The macroscopic polarisation at the probe frequency is proportional to atomic number density times a transition dipole expectation, often related to ρge. Susceptibility χ follows only after applying the correct dipole normalisation and optical frequency convention. Propagation through a medium depends on the complex refractive index; absorption and phase are distinct observables. A raw coherence plotted against laser detuning is *not* yet an oscilloscope voltage, nor does it include finite optical depth, cell windows, photodetection, beam geometry or servo drift. Distinguish susceptibility, normalised absorption, transmission fraction and calibrated volts in plot titles.

## 6. Thermal averaging and physical rates

A warm vapour contains atoms with velocity v distributed approximately by Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics. Each beam experiences Doppler shifts from k·v, with sign dictated by beam propagation, so a two-photon resonance retains residual Doppler sensitivity when wavelengths differ. Transit broadening depends on beam size and thermal velocity, blackbody transitions couple nearby Rydberg levels and can shorten effective lifetime, and collisions or optical pumping may introduce state-changing rates. Add each mechanism with a justified independent parameter, then perform velocity-grid and truncation convergence tests.

## 7. Worked matrix example

For ρ=[[0.7,0.2],[0.2,0.3]], trace is one, purity is 0.7²+0.3²+2×0.2²=0.66, and eigenvalues are approximately 0.7828 and 0.2172, hence physical. Completely dephase off-diagonal elements while preserving populations: ρ′=diag(0.7,0.3), purity falls to 0.58. A Z-basis measurement sees no change, while an X-basis measurement loses its original coherence-dependent bias. The example shows that incoherent ensembles with the same populations can have different spectroscopic responses.

## 8. A validation ladder for any optical Bloch code

Start with a two-level analytic limit. Add a third state and show the optical-coupling-off limit. Verify positivity, trace and residual at each detuning. Increase truncation until line shapes converge. For a thermal cell, double the Doppler quadrature resolution and report both the velocity span and convergence difference. When using a solver package, record its version, detuning units, decoherence conventions and exact state graph. Only after the physical observable is calibrated against independent data should a fitted RF field be described as a measurement.

## End-of-chapter questions and fully explained answers

### Problem 1. What are the basic physical conditions on ρ?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Hermiticity, positivity and unit trace. Purity is an additional diagnostic of whether a state is mixed.

</details>

### Problem 2. Why does a pure-dephasing jump alter EIT?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It damps coherence needed for interference, potentially destroying transparency even when level populations change little.

</details>

### Problem 3. How can a steady state fail to be unique?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Disconnected or symmetry-protected subspaces can support multiple stationary density matrices; inspect the Liouvillian nullspace.

</details>

### Problem 4. Why is Imρge not automatically equal to photodetector current?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

One must calculate susceptibility, propagate the optical field and include detector responsivity, amplification and calibration.

</details>

### Problem 5. How does a Doppler integral differ from adding a constant linewidth?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It averages detuning-dependent responses over physical velocity classes, potentially yielding non-Lorentzian profiles.

</details>

### Problem 6. Why does coherence decay at Γ/2 in simple spontaneous emission?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

A population-decay jump attenuates the excited-state amplitude at half the population rate, yielding a Γ/2 optical-coherence damping contribution.

</details>

### Problem 7. What are minimum numerical checks for a solver?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Trace, Hermiticity, positivity, Liouvillian residual, convergence versus basis truncation and the relevant analytic limits.

</details>

### Problem 8. Why must the temperature be specified in a Rydberg lifetime calculation?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Blackbody-induced transitions and thermal populations depend on temperature, so an isolated radiative lifetime need not be the effective experiment lifetime.

</details>

## Advanced practical assignment

Implement a minimal self-contained version of the chapter's central equation. Supply its units, analytic limiting cases, a second independent check, and a reproducible test that fails when a sign or unit is changed. Distinguish generated illustrations from laboratory data. Explain how the model would be extended to a specific atomic species *only after* those foundations are correct.

## References

Use [F1] Foot, [Q1] Scully and Zubairy, [F2] Steck's Quantum and Atom Optics and the numerical analysis sources in [the bibliography](../REFERENCES.md). Consult original primary publications before reusing a parameter as experimental evidence.

title: Atomic angular momentum and transition selection rules

# Atomic angular momentum and transition selection rules

**General atomic and quantum physics textbook.** The treatment is not a project-specific apparatus description. Physics constants and state labels must be verified for each chosen species.

## Learning objectives

Derive the central equations, quantify assumptions, compute a simple limiting case, plan an independent experiment and diagnose numerical or laboratory errors.

## 1. Quantum numbers and coupling schemes

Electron orbital angular momentum L combines with spin S to form J, while nuclear spin I couples with J to form F. Magnetic projections are m_J and m_F in their respective bases. The allowed j values range from |l−s| to l+s; for alkalis s=1/2. A state label n,l,j is not sufficient to describe resolved hyperfine spectroscopy, and strong magnetic fields can invalidate the F-coupled basis by mixing manifolds. Always state the quantisation axis and the regime of field coupling.

## 2. Electric dipole selection rules

For electric-dipole E1 transitions, parity changes and Δl=±1 in a nonrelativistic one-electron description. Spherical components q=−1,0,+1 change magnetic projection by Δm=q when defined consistently. The triangle rule restricts angular momentum, and a J=0↔J′=0 E1 transition is forbidden. Hyperfine selection rules usually allow ΔF=0,±1 except F=0↔0, subject to the relevant approximations. Violating a selection rule can make a large radial integral irrelevant.

## 3. Clebsch–Gordan and Wigner coefficients

A dipole matrix element separates radial and angular parts using Wigner–Eckart theorem. The reduced matrix element captures much of the electronic structure, while 3j/6j coefficients describe projections and recoupling. Different phase conventions can flip the sign of an individual matrix element without altering absolute transition strengths, but relative phases are crucial in interference. Compare coefficient conventions before mixing ARC, spectroscopy tables and independent quantum simulators.

## 4. Zeeman and Breit–Rabi regimes

For weak field in a definite hyperfine manifold a linear approximation ΔE≈g_F μB m_F B may apply. At larger field the electron and nuclear angular momenta decouple gradually and a Breit–Rabi-like description is required for the relevant levels. Rydberg states can also have Stark mixing and core effects. A sharp magnetic spectral feature is not proof of a particular m-state until optical and RF reference conditions are controlled.

## 5. Angular components of an RF wave

Write a complex electric field in the coordinate system tied to quantisation axis. π drives q=0 components and σ± drive the corresponding circular spherical components under a declared time convention. Reversing propagation direction or changing e^{-iωt} to e^{+iωt} can invert handedness labels. A linear RF antenna generally excites a superposition of σ+ and σ− if its field is transverse to the magnetic axis.

## 6. Worked angular selection example

From j=1/2,m=+1/2 to j′=3/2,m′=+3/2 requires q=+1; to m′=−3/2 would require q=−2 and is forbidden for a single E1 photon. A radial matrix element could be large but the forbidden magnetic transition must be rejected. Enumerate allowed values before computing frequencies or assigning an observed optical peak.

## End-of-chapter review questions and worked answers

### Question 1. What changes if the quantisation axis rotates?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

The spherical decomposition of a fixed laboratory electric field and thus observed transition couplings.

</details>

### Question 2. Why is a dipole radial integral not a complete strength?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Angular selection and Wigner coefficients may zero or weight the physical transition.

</details>

### Question 3. Which q couples Δm=−1?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

The spherical component conventionally labelled σ−, assuming the stated quantisation and phase conventions.

</details>

### Question 4. When is F a poor approximate quantum number?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

When magnetic-field mixing makes hyperfine coupling no longer dominant.

</details>

### Question 5. Does a right-circular optical label imply the same RF q in every frame?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

No; propagation and time-phase conventions must be aligned.

</details>

### Question 6. Why must a state be fully labelled?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

n,l,j alone may hide important m or hyperfine degeneracies and selection rules.

</details>

## Graduate practical problem

Develop a reproducible calculation for the principal equation in this chapter, record coordinate frame and units, compare against a separate source or an analytically solvable limit, and describe a controlled measurement that could falsify the model. Explicitly distinguish a derived teaching example from new experimental evidence.

## Scholarly sources

See [the textbook bibliography](../REFERENCES.md), Gallagher (*Rydberg Atoms*), Foot (*Atomic Physics*), Scully and Zubairy (*Quantum Optics*), and official atomic spectroscopy data when applying formulas to an actual species.

title: Rydberg energy levels, lifetimes and scaling laws
markdown:
# Rydberg energy levels, lifetimes and scaling laws

**General atomic and quantum physics textbook.** The treatment is not a project-specific apparatus description. Physics constants and state labels must be verified for each chosen species.

## Learning objectives

Derive the central equations, quantify assumptions, compute a simple limiting case, plan an independent experiment and diagnose numerical or laboratory errors.

## 1. Hydrogenic intuition and the effective quantum number

High-lying bound electrons have large spatial extent and small binding energies. A hydrogenic reference obeys E_n≈−hcR*/n², but an alkali valence electron penetrates its ionic core and experiences a quantum defect δ_{lj}. Replacing n with n*=n−δ_{lj} improves level-energy estimates. The defect varies by angular state and can be energy dependent; one fitted value cannot replace actual atomic data across all series.

## 2. Deriving transition-frequency scaling

For neighbouring high-n levels, differentiate E∝−1/(n*)² to obtain ΔE∝(n*)^{−3} as a leading scaling. Therefore raising n often brings neighbouring Rydberg transitions into lower microwave bands. The law is approximate: fine structure, quantum defects, near-degenerate manifolds and external fields can change individual lines. Compare predicted levels against ARC or precision spectroscopy before selecting hardware.

## 3. Orbital extent and polarizability

The typical radial scale grows roughly as n*² a0. Static polarizability in suitable nondegenerate high-n regimes can increase steeply, often with an approximate n*^7 scale, while resonantly enhanced dipole response depends on particular neighbouring states. Large polarizability brings sensitivity and vulnerability: stray DC charge on nearby windows may shift or mix states enough to spoil an optical ladder.

## 4. Lifetimes and blackbody radiation

Ideal high-n radiative lifetimes often scale approximately as n*³, but room-temperature blackbody photons drive adjacent Rydberg transitions and can change effective population loss. State mixing, collisions and surface proximity add further channels. Distinguish zero-temperature spontaneous radiative lifetime from temperature-dependent effective lifetime returned by atomic libraries. If optical transit time is much shorter than a radiative lifetime, transit decoherence may dominate the experiment.

## 5. Scaling the interaction regime

Two Rydberg atoms can interact through resonant dipole–dipole V∝R^{−3} or perturbative van der Waals V∝R^{−6}. The interaction coefficient often scales steeply with principal quantum number, but actual angular channels and Förster defects matter. Extrapolating an interaction at one n into another without verifying channel mixing risks a large error. Use pair-state diagonalisation when the perturbative denominator becomes small.

## 6. Quantitative thought experiment

For n* increasing from 70 to 90, the adjacent-spacing ratio is approximately (70/90)^3≈0.4705. That does not imply every line moves down by exactly 53 percent or that all lifetimes scale identically. Verify with explicit quantum defects, angular momenta and atom-specific constants. A credible transition table includes n,l,j,m, frequency, dipole projection, upper/lower lifetime, optical access and magnetic sensitivity.

## End-of-chapter review questions and worked answers

### Question 1. How does adjacent spacing scale in a simple high-n series?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

As (n*)^{−3} to leading order.

</details>

### Question 2. Why does a high-n atom sense stray fields strongly?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Its large electronic extent and dense neighbouring levels yield enhanced polarizability and dipole response.

</details>

### Question 3. Is a quantum defect the same for s and high-l states?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

No, core penetration strongly depends on orbital angular momentum.

</details>

### Question 4. Which lifetime should be used in warm vapour?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

A temperature- and environment-appropriate effective lifetime, not blindly the zero-K radiative result.

</details>

### Question 5. When is a van der Waals coefficient invalid?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

Near resonant pair-state mixing or outside perturbative separation/basis conditions.

</details>

### Question 6. Can a scaling law establish exact optical access?

<details><summary>Show explained solution</summary>

No; use state-specific quantum defects and measured laser range.

</details>

## Graduate practical problem

Develop a reproducible calculation for the principal equation in this chapter, record coordinate frame and units, compare against a separate source or an analytically solvable limit, and describe a controlled measurement that could falsify the model. Explicitly distinguish a derived teaching example from new experimental evidence.

## Scholarly sources

See [the textbook bibliography](../REFERENCES.md), Gallagher (*Rydberg Atoms*), Foot (*Atomic Physics*), Scully and Zubairy (*Quantum Optics*), and official atomic spectroscopy data when applying formulas to an actual species.

title: Alkali excitation ladders and spectroscopic access
markdown:
# Alkali excitation ladders and spectroscopic access

**General Rydberg and optical physics chapter.** Species and apparatus choices are examples, not a report of one project.

## Competencies

Derive the optical and atomic response, identify the real observable, use state-specific data, design controls, and discriminate physical behaviour from technical artefacts.

## 1. Choosing a legitimate ladder

An alkali Rydberg excitation scheme moves population or coherence from the ground state to a highly excited manifold using one or more photons. A common thermal-vapour ladder involves 5S→5P→nS/nD for rubidium, but the actual intermediate and final states depend on isotope, hyperfine level, polarisation and tuning resources. Approximate wavelengths are useful for orientation, never a substitute for a state-specific level table. Some elements require UV sources, two-photon excitation or alternative intermediate levels, and cold platforms may avoid the same ladder architecture entirely.

## 2. Selection rules in every stage

Write each step with n,l,j,F,m where resolved. Apply parity and Δl=±1 to electric-dipole transitions, together with magnetic projection selection under the chosen quantisation axis. A laser nominally tuned to an allowed line may be ineffective when its polarisation projects weakly onto the accessible transition or when optical pumping empties the initial sublevel. The Rabi rate depends on the specific dipole matrix element and electric-field amplitude, not simply the optical power printed on the laser.

## 3. Wavelength, detuning and Doppler reference

The frequency of light in vacuum is f=c/λ; two-photon detuning combines optical frequencies and state energies with their signs. For a moving atom, each beam contributes k·v to its detuning. Whether beams co- or counterpropagate matters to the residual Doppler width. Laser beam crossing angle, cell refractive index, wavemeter calibration and scan nonlinearity should be recorded. A 780 nm laser is hundreds of terahertz in carrier frequency, while scanning a few megahertz concerns a tiny relative shift.

## 4. Coherent and incoherent coupling

An ideal three-state ladder has probe and coupling Rabi frequencies, one-photon and two-photon detunings, intermediate decay and Rydberg dephasing. Strong coupling can dress eigenstates and modify absorption. Incoherent pumping, transit relaxation and hyperfine branching can change population distributions. A single optical trace cannot separately identify every rate without independent controls, making physically informed parameter priors and additional measurements necessary.

## 5. Practical screening with ARC

Begin with a table of candidate Rydberg n,l,j states. Query ARC for actual energies, transition frequencies, dipole matrix elements and lifetime, checking the returned frequency sign and units. Reject inaccessible laser transitions or forbidden magnetic pathways. For a warm-vapour receiver, then calculate Doppler broadening and the optical susceptibility with a consistent density-matrix model. Export source code and a machine-readable table; do not derive all conclusions from a screenshot of an energy-level diagram.

## 6. What to do when nothing appears

Check the ground and intermediate hyperfine lock, optical overlap, beam propagation, coupling polarisation and temperature. Confirm the detector is linear and the scan actually passes through two-photon resonance. Use coupling-off and RF-off baselines, and compare source frequency changes with the optical feature. Only after these controls are verified should unusual physics be invoked.

## 7. Worked wavelength interpretation

For the rubidium D2 transition, accurate spectroscopy tables place the vacuum wavelength near 780.241 nm, while an air wavelength is near 780.033 nm. The difference arises because wavelength depends on the medium but frequency does not. Mistaking the two values, or using a wavemeter configured to a different convention, can confuse coarse tuning and line assignment. Always cite the isotope and vacuum/air convention.

## End-of-chapter questions with answers

### Question 1. Can two lasers with the right approximate wavelengths guarantee EIT?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

No; transition selection, locks, coherence, beam overlap, Doppler conditions, power and decays must also be correct.

</details>

### Question 2. Why are optical transition frequencies signed in atomic software?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

They indicate ordering of initial and final energy levels; magnitude is not sufficient to determine the direction of a process.

</details>

### Question 3. How does a counterpropagating geometry affect two-photon Doppler shift?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

It changes the relative sign of k·v terms and often reduces residual broadening in unequal-wavelength ladders.

</details>

### Question 4. Why can a nominally allowed transition be dark?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Population may occupy other magnetic sublevels or light polarisation may not couple the desired projection.

</details>

### Question 5. What is the difference between vacuum and air wavelength?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Frequency remains fixed while phase velocity and wavelength depend on refractive index.

</details>

### Question 6. What must an optical ladder table include?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

State labels, frequency, laser access, dipole projection, detuning, linewidth and lifetime assumptions.

</details>

## Practical scientific assignment

Construct a species-labelled excitation ladder and optical-signal model, calculate the required photon or RF frequency using verified data, and design a control sequence that separates optical drift, detector effects and atomic response. Record assumptions, uncertainties, raw data provenance and expected failure signatures.

## Sources

Foot, *Atomic Physics*; Scully and Zubairy, *Quantum Optics*; Steck spectroscopy data; RydIQule and ARC official guides; and the [book bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

title: Electromagnetically induced transparency and dressed-state spectroscopy
markdown:
# Electromagnetically induced transparency and dressed-state spectroscopy

**General Rydberg and optical physics chapter.** Species and apparatus choices are examples, not a report of one project.

## Competencies

Derive the optical and atomic response, identify the real observable, use state-specific data, design controls, and discriminate physical behaviour from technical artefacts.

## 1. Absorption without coupling

A weak probe near an optical transition is absorbed according to the ensemble susceptibility and propagation length. In a simplified two-level response, coherence between ground and excited states has a Lorentzian-like resonance controlled by decay and detuning. The measured transmission follows a propagation law and depends on atom density, optical depth and detector gain. A toy coherence calculated in arbitrary units should not be labelled volts or measured intensity.

## 2. How transparency emerges

A second coherent optical field couples the excited state to an upper state and creates competing excitation pathways. At appropriate two-photon resonance, destructive interference can suppress excitation of the lossy intermediate state and produce a narrow transparency feature. It is a quantum-coherence effect, not a hole drilled in the absorption medium. In an ideal weak-probe ladder model, the optical coherence contains a nested denominator involving intermediate decoherence, upper-state decoherence and coupling Rabi frequency; the exact sign convention must be stated.

## 3. EIT versus Autler–Townes splitting

A strong resonant coupling dresses two levels and can create resolvable absorption peaks separated on the scale of its Rabi frequency. EIT and AT are related, but their regimes and interference interpretations differ. When peaks overlap due to decay, Doppler broadening or finite spectral resolution, fitting two peaks may not yield a trustworthy splitting. Evidence of a field-induced spectroscopic feature is stronger when its scaling with source amplitude, detuning and optical controls agrees with a parameterised forward model.

## 4. Adding microwave coupling

An RF drive couples two Rydberg states, further modifying the optical dressed-state spectrum. In the simplest resonant two-level limit, Ω_RF=|μ·E|/ℏ. That correspondence is not automatically a measured field strength: the dipole projection, RF detuning, magnetic sublevels, optical propagation and detector response affect the inferred spectrum. Arbitrary elliptic RF fields can excite multiple σ and π pathways and produce complex multiplet structures beyond a cartoon doublet.

## 5. Thermal cells, velocity classes and optical depth

Each moving atom sees Doppler-shifted probe and coupling detunings; measured absorption is a velocity-weighted sum. Counterpropagating beams can reduce residual two-photon Doppler width but not eliminate unequal-wavelength effects. Transit relaxation, laser linewidth, optical pumping and Rydberg blackbody transfers may broaden or distort transparency. Optically thick samples require propagation, and a spatially varying RF field makes the detector integrate heterogeneous atomic responses.

## 6. A minimal four-condition validation

Acquire identical-gain spectra with the RF off/on and the coherent coupling light off/on. A claimed Rydberg-origin RF feature should be absent or significantly altered when the ladder coherence cannot exist. Independently check optical laser frequency, source RF power and carrier spectrum; repeat at multiple field amplitudes. Archive raw scans and fit residuals instead of only a smoothed overlay.

## 7. Numerical thought experiment

Take a resonant Ω_c/2π of several MHz and a Rydberg coherence decay much narrower than intermediate-state linewidth. A weak probe may show a narrow transparency feature if two-photon resonance and selection rules permit. If the upper coherence decay increases until comparable with optical coupling, contrast falls and a clear EIT window may disappear. This qualitative result can be tested by solving the actual Lindblad equations rather than assuming a perfect dark state at every temperature.

## End-of-chapter questions with answers

### Question 1. What physically causes EIT?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Coherent excitation-path interference suppresses absorption through the lossy intermediate state at suitable resonance.

</details>

### Question 2. Why can unresolved AT peaks occur despite RF coupling?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

The dressed splitting can be smaller than linewidth, Doppler and spectral resolution.

</details>

### Question 3. Is a pair of optical peaks proof of microwave field amplitude?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

No; proper state matrix element, detuning, propagation and calibration are required.

</details>

### Question 4. What distinguishes RF-on coupling-off control?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

It helps identify non-Rydberg optical/electronic artefacts that persist without the coherent ladder.

</details>

### Question 5. Why do thermal velocities matter?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Each velocity class experiences a different detuning; the ensemble response is an integral, not a single stationary atom.

</details>

### Question 6. Why should spectra be fit to an optical observable rather than raw ρge?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Detector transmission includes susceptibility propagation, optical depth and gain.

</details>

## Practical scientific assignment

Construct a species-labelled excitation ladder and optical-signal model, calculate the required photon or RF frequency using verified data, and design a control sequence that separates optical drift, detector effects and atomic response. Record assumptions, uncertainties, raw data provenance and expected failure signatures.

## Sources

Foot, *Atomic Physics*; Scully and Zubairy, *Quantum Optics*; Steck spectroscopy data; RydIQule and ARC official guides; and the [book bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

title: Optical engineering, detection and alignment
markdown:
# Optical engineering, detection and alignment

**General Rydberg and optical physics chapter.** Species and apparatus choices are examples, not a report of one project.

## Competencies

Derive the optical and atomic response, identify the real observable, use state-specific data, design controls, and discriminate physical behaviour from technical artefacts.

## 1. Optical power and field amplitude

A Gaussian TEM00 beam with optical power P and waist w0 has peak intensity I0=2P/(πw0²) under the standard 1/e² intensity radius definition. In free space the root-mean-square electric field relates to intensity through I=cε0 E_rms². A Rabi rate follows the transition dipole projection times field amplitude divided by ℏ. If the quoted power is measured before an acousto-optic modulator, cell window or fibre, include losses before predicting on-atom coupling.

## 2. Beam propagation and overlap

Gaussian beam radius evolves as w(z)=w0√(1+(z/zR)²), where zR=πw0²/λ. Lens aberration, astigmatism and clipping can invalidate an ideal paraxial model. In a vapour cell, optical probe and coupling overlap must be maintained over an adequate interaction length; crossing angle affects both volume and Doppler geometry. In a tweezer experiment, high numerical aperture and accurate intensity distribution define trap confinement and addressing fidelity.

## 3. Polarisation preparation

Waveplates produce phase delays between orthogonal optical axes, while polarising beam splitters and analysers distinguish projections. A quarter-wave plate generates ideal circular light only for the correct incident linear state, axis setting and wavelength. Birefringent windows, stress and magnetic-field orientation can change the actual polarisation at the atoms. For magnetic sublevel selection, polarisation must be defined relative to the quantisation axis, not just the appearance of a laboratory arrow.

## 4. Photodetection and electronics

A photodiode current is I_pd=R(λ)P_opt in its linear regime. Transimpedance gain converts current to voltage, while amplifier bandwidth and noise contribute to the measured time series. Overload, feedback instability or a dark offset may distort spectroscopy. Determine whether the oscilloscope is sampling slowly varying optical scan intensity, RF-beat modulation or the raw optical carrier; ordinary photodiodes do not time-resolve hundreds of terahertz optical oscillations.

## 5. Laser frequency stability and diagnostics

Separate fast and slow frequency noise, free-running linewidth, long-term lock drift and absolute reference uncertainty. Saturation absorption, etalon, beat note and wavemeter measurements probe different properties; an in-loop error signal does not independently establish an out-of-loop optical linewidth. Document frequency calibration, scan direction, dwell time, servo state, optical powers and reference frequency for every scientific trace.

## 6. A practical alignment validation sequence

With institutional laser safety controls, identify probe and coupling beam paths separately; verify power, mode quality and detector gain. Establish baseline absorption with probe only, then add coupling at a known resonance and adjust overlap while retaining raw references. Repeat at lower power to test saturation and broadenings. For an RF-controlled experiment, introduce RF only after stable EIT is confirmed, so optical and RF faults do not become entangled in diagnosis.

## End-of-chapter questions with answers

### Question 1. How does peak Gaussian intensity change when w0 halves?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

It increases fourfold at constant power under an ideal TEM00 model.

</details>

### Question 2. Why is a detector output not an optical carrier waveform?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Photodiode bandwidth generally follows envelope/modulation, not the optical hundreds-of-terahertz carrier.

</details>

### Question 3. What changes a waveplate's ideal phase retardance?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Wavelength, crystal properties, incidence and temperature may shift the designed retardance.

</details>

### Question 4. Why does a laser lock's error trace not prove absolute frequency stability?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

It can remain quiet while its reference drifts or common-mode errors occur.

</details>

### Question 5. What optical measurements should precede RF coupling?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Stable probe absorption, laser references, coupling-dependent EIT, power, overlap and linear detector response.

</details>

### Question 6. Why can reducing waist worsen EIT in a vapour?

<details><summary>Reveal the worked answer</summary>

Transit time shortens, increasing motional decoherence despite greater intensity.

</details>

## Practical scientific assignment

Construct a species-labelled excitation ladder and optical-signal model, calculate the required photon or RF frequency using verified data, and design a control sequence that separates optical drift, detector effects and atomic response. Record assumptions, uncertainties, raw data provenance and expected failure signatures.

## Sources

Foot, *Atomic Physics*; Scully and Zubairy, *Quantum Optics*; Steck spectroscopy data; RydIQule and ARC official guides; and the [book bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

title: Electromagnetic waves, RF hardware and atomic field coupling
markdown:
# Electromagnetic waves, RF hardware and atomic field coupling

**General graduate textbook chapter**, applicable to optical, microwave and Rydberg systems without relying on any one research project.

## Outcomes

Derive the core relations, identify measurement conventions, construct a reproducible model, calculate a limiting case and identify a false-positive result.

## 1. From Maxwell equations to plane waves

Maxwell equations relate electric displacement, magnetic flux, conduction current and charge. In a homogeneous lossless medium, a monochromatic plane wave has k=ω√(με), its transverse E and H fields are related through impedance η=√(μ/ε), and free-space wavelength is λ0=c/f. The time-averaged Poynting flux of peak phasors is Re(E×H*)/2; using RMS field phasors omits the one-half factor. This convention matters when converting calibrated power into a local electric-field amplitude.

## 2. Near field versus far field

A source does not produce a uniform plane wave at every distance. Reactive and radiative field components decay differently; the geometric relationship between antenna size, wavelength and observation distance controls whether a plane-wave or far-field approximation is justified. A compact cell near a radiating element can experience complex spatially varying fields and longitudinal components. The plane-wave port S parameters of an isolated microwave component do not by themselves determine the atom-local electric field.

## 3. Network analyzers and reference planes

Scattering parameters relate incident and reflected travelling-wave amplitudes at specified characteristic impedances. A vector network analyzer must be calibrated to a reference plane through cables, connectors and fixtures. S21 magnitude gives transmission under its port and load conventions; a polarisation-sensitive local-field model also needs complex phase and vector components. Incoherent subtraction of dB values or mixing power and voltage logarithms can give wrong extinction ratios.

## 4. Power calibration and antenna pattern

For power P in watts, dBm=10log10(P/1mW). A 3 dB power change is approximately a factor two in power but only √2 in electric-field amplitude for fixed impedance. Antenna gain, polarisation mismatch and path loss must be applied in their correct domains. A high-gain antenna pointed at a cell is not proof of an incident plane-wave field: scattering from optical mounts and cell windows may substantially change local direction and handedness.

## 5. RF coupling to an atomic dipole

The coupling is Ω=|⟨i|d·E|j⟩|/ℏ. The complex vector E includes phase and orientation, and the transition dipole is defined in an atomic state basis. Rotating the magnetic quantisation axis changes which spherical component drives a particular m transition. RF polarization, noise and frequency modulation can therefore alter atomic optical spectra even at the same total received RF power.

## 6. Hardware fault isolation

When an optical atomic response seems absent, independently inspect source generator power/carrier, antenna/cable reference, RF detuning from the atomic transition, field orientation and optical EIT. Avoid blaming an antenna solely from a zero optical detector contrast; atoms may be prepared in an uncoupled sublevel or the optical linewidth may be too broad. Preserve VNA calibration kits, source spectra, power units, layout drawings and detector data separately.

## End-of-chapter questions and explained answers

### Question 1. What does S21 measure?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Complex port transmission under a specified impedance and calibration reference, not necessarily local atom-cell field.

</details>

### Question 2. What is free-space wavelength at 2 GHz?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Approximately 0.150 m using c/f.

</details>

### Question 3. Why can a dB voltage ratio use 20log but a power ratio 10log?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Power is quadratic in field/voltage for a fixed impedance.

</details>

### Question 4. Why might atoms see different field polarisation from an antenna datasheet?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Nearby structures and finite observation geometry can scatter the field and change complex components.

</details>

### Question 5. How does RF field orientation enter atomic Rabi frequency?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Through the vector dipole projection and allowed spherical components.

</details>

### Question 6. What must be written beside a VNA plot?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Reference planes, S-parameter definition, ports/impedance, calibration state, frequency and phase conventions.

</details>

title: Jones, Stokes, Mueller and full-vector polarisation

# Jones, Stokes, Mueller and full-vector polarisation

**General graduate textbook chapter**, applicable to optical, microwave and Rydberg systems without relying on any one research project.

## Outcomes

Derive the core relations, identify measurement conventions, construct a reproducible model, calculate a limiting case and identify a false-positive result.

## 1. What a Jones vector describes

For a monochromatic coherent transverse field propagating along a declared axis, the Jones vector is J=(Ex,Ey)ᵀ with complex phasor components. It captures relative phase and amplitudes but requires a fixed overall phase convention. A detector measuring |Ex|² and |Ey|² alone does not recover their relative phase. An arbitrary partially polarised field is more generally described by a coherency matrix, not a single deterministic Jones vector.

## 2. Derive the Stokes coordinates

One valid convention for e^{−iωt} phasors defines S0=|Ex|²+|Ey|², S1=|Ex|²−|Ey|², S2=2Re(ExEy*), S3=2Im(ExEy*). Some RF and optical references reverse the sign of S3; never mix labels from two conventions without an explicit transformation. For a deterministic pure Jones state, S1²+S2²+S3²=S0². For a partially polarised statistical field, the inequality becomes ≤S0², and the degree of polarisation is the ratio of three-coordinate magnitude to S0.

## 3. Geometric interpretation

Normalized (s1,s2,s3) lies on the Poincaré sphere for pure polarisation and inside it for mixtures. Linear states lie along the equator, circular states at poles and elliptical states between. A linear polariser rotated through all possible angles can constrain some linear projections but cannot resolve the sign of circular handedness by itself. A device claiming full-Stokes must provide enough independent polarization-sensitive measurements and a calibrated forward map.

## 4. Polarisation optics and Mueller matrices

A deterministic Jones matrix transforms field amplitudes, whereas a Mueller matrix transforms Stokes vectors of fields including partial polarization. The latter is a real 4×4 representation but is not simply identical to a classical sensor's arbitrary 6×4 observation matrix. Loss, depolarisation and phase retardation must be modeled appropriately; a diagonal gain factor can shift observed Stokes values without changing the underlying incident polarisation.

## 5. Measurement bases and inverse models

A set of analysed intensity measurements can be written y=AS+ε when a calibrated linear Stokes observation model applies. At least four linearly independent rows are needed to reconstruct four real Stokes coordinates noiselessly; adding more rows may improve noise robustness but not guarantee accuracy. For a partially polarised field, positivity of the coherency matrix imposes S0≥√(S1²+S2²+S3²) and S0≥0. A least-squares solution outside the physical cone signals noise or model error.

## 6. Worked circular-state example

Choose Ex=1/√2 and Ey=i/√2. Under the defined formula, ExEy*=−i/2, so S=(1,0,0,−1). Reversing the sign of Ey flips S3 to +1 while leaving S0,S1,S2 identical. Therefore any measurement insensitive to relative phase cannot distinguish these states; the experiment must add circular/elliptical sensitivity. Helicity naming depends on the propagation and time convention, so the numbers are more reliable than an unlabeled 'RHCP' arrow.

## End-of-chapter questions and explained answers

### Question 1. Why is S3 convention sensitive?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Its sign depends on the phasor time dependence and the circular-handedness/propagation definition.

</details>

### Question 2. What is missing from a rotated linear-polarizer measurement?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Independent sensitivity to relative phase and thus circular handedness.

</details>

### Question 3. Can a mixed field be described by one Jones vector?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Not generally; use the ensemble coherency matrix and Stokes parameters.

</details>

### Question 4. What is the physical cone for Stokes vectors?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

S0≥0 and S0²≥S1²+S2²+S3².

</details>

### Question 5. Why is a Mueller matrix not identical to any 6×4 detector matrix?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

The former maps four Stokes coordinates to four Stokes coordinates; a detector matrix maps Stokes coordinates to distinct calibrated observations.

</details>

### Question 6. How do you validate a measured Stokes sign?

<details><summary>Show complete answer</summary>

Use known elliptical/circular reference inputs and a declared propagation/time convention.

</details>
